ideaflow/2026-02-16/consciousness.html.title: consciousness
ideaflow/2026-02-16/consciousness.html.description: consciousnessThe idea of becoming conscious, or, you know, becoming a gentic, or, like, understanding the world around you and yourself, is it interesting that thing that I could probably write about? I think a good framing is like, you know, something like on becoming conscious, right? I think it's fairly understandable, and... the certain things inside are fairly explainable. I think a couple aspects outline what I think I mean by this. One is, like, you know, understand... Sorry. Understanding of yourself, right? There are definitely many tears of this. Especially the world. I mean, that's easier to explain. First, here is, like, what the fuck is the world, right? Like, you're not aware that there is such a thing as, like, an environment and, you know, you're not aware that there's a separation between you and the environment, and you can do certain things. Um... So that definitely kind of ties into, like, the understanding of you, uh, and your relationship to the environment. These are all kind of related. Um, and then there's, uh... a understanding which is like, Oh, yeah, there is an environment, and, you know, you're in it, and you do things, right? And then there's a understanding of like, how does the environment work? Like, what happens when you do certain actions? What happens when other people do certain actions? What happens when other things sue certain actions? Like, are there predictable patterns? And, you know, yes, there are. And then there are higher levels of understanding that are like, what are the dynamics that arise? When there are people like us, and when there are environments such as the one that we have? et cetera. And there are more higher dimensions as well. And then there's, like, the self understanding, and I think self understanding is the most important of, like, self goals as well. Like, you know, like, you're in this world, and you're acting, and you're like, Why am I acting? Like, why do I do the things that I do? Um, is there for some goal or something? Um, I think that's a part of being conscious as well. And then there's kind of, like, opinions, you know, strategies for existing the world and interacting with other people. #towrite

writing/a_glimpse_into_consciousness.htm.title: a_glimpse_into_consciousness
writing/a_glimpse_into_consciousness.htm.description:
At the beginning of this semester, my Computational Biology teacher posed a big question to us: What is life?[1] Throughout my time in this class, biology, and in my everyday life, I have constantly been pondering this question. My current hypothesis is that life is easily explainable, understandable, and logical. However, one thing about life still eludes me: consciousness. The idea of consciousness has been discussed at length all the way back in the time of ancient philosophers like Plato and Aristotle. In this essay, I will describe different interpretations of consciousness, my understanding of consciousness from both an evolutionary and philosophical standpoint, as well as my thoughts and aspirations for it.Firstly, consciousness is not an idea that only has one definition. In terms of semantics, it means understanding, awareness, and having knowledge. In terms of functionality, it can be a basic ability to perceive the world, remember the world, and react to it, often classified as lower consciousness, or the ability to understand abstract ideas like language, self, and feelings, often classified as higher consciousness. Note that these interpretations are used in fields that only care about the functional value of consciousness, or, in other words, the outside observable attributes of a conscious being. For the sake of avoiding confusion, I will call this “functional consciousness” which I intend to be synonymous with behaviorism. There is another interpretation that involves a philosophical idea that is much less quantifiable: qualia. Qualia is the subjective sensation that a conscious being experiences. I like to think of it as the intricate gaming interface that your many senses and muscles create for you; as if you were a player in an expansive digital world. In this way, you sense things very differently from what can be quantified and observed from the outside. When a tiger leaps towards you, many signals are sent to your brain. However, instead of feeling that signal or feeling many neurons firing in your brain, you see the tiger in a very intuitive and direct way. This I will call “sensory consciousness”, also for the sake of avoiding confusion.
Just like many other parts of life, functional consciousness can be explained plainly through the analysis of biological systems and their evolutionary processes. Through natural selection, different self-sustaining organisms change in ways that are reproductively favorable.[2] Throughout this process, many beneficial traits are selected for, such as wings, eyes, tails, arms, and most importantly, brains.[3] I’m not an expert on this, so I won’t pretend to be, but I’m pretty sure that the majority of successful large scale organisms today have brains (even the dinosaurs!). This follows the same logic: brains are prominent because they helped organisms outcompete competition and reproduce successfully. While brains are not synonymous with functional consciousness, it can be observed that species with brains need their brains for their functional consciousness.In stark contrast, sensory consciousness is basically impossible to analyze quantitatively. This is because of the way qualia is defined: the subjective experience. Termed “the hard problem”, it is a mostly abstract and unapproachable concept that is discussed mainly in philosophy and separate from other experimental sciences. Thought experiments like the philosophical zombie or china brain exemplifies this gap by constructing scenarios where a being exhibits intelligent behavior such as normal human actions or computational complexity, but does not experience a consciousness corresponding to its being. Many different attempts have been made to make sense of this phenomenon, but they have all failed to provide a uniform, generalizable, and unassuming theory. Current day theories rely on making bold assumptions about aspects of consciousness to make hypotheses.
While it is difficult, the problem of sensory consciousness is surprisingly interesting to me because it is so elusive. Functional consciousness is explainable and logical, but sensory consciousness is just mysterious. Having modeled the parts of the brain in Ted’s class and conducted research for this essay, I have seen the value of brain models as well as personally felt many of the frustrations that people across time and space have run into trying to study this phenomenon.[4] For example, in the neuroscience module, we studied aspects of the Integrated Information Theory[5] in relation to consciousness. I liked this approach because it relates to functional consciousness in its connection to computational complexity, which is observed through behaviors of the system. It essentially postulates that when a system is complex enough—showing attributes like integration, differentiation, and reentry—it will be conscious, and to measure this, we analyze its behavior, such as its intellectual abilities, reaction to certain stimulation, or information representation capabilities. In no way is it a general theory of consciousness, but it is interesting because it connects these two ideas of consciousness like a bridge.
Furthermore, this problem is intimate to every single human being on earth.[6] We experience qualia everyday, and are taught that it is constructed purely from our sensory organs. The first time I was introduced to this idea, I was baffled. I mean, it sounds completely insane that the ultra-sensory VR video game we call life is actually just created by some electrical signals in our flesh.[7] Where are all the wires and display screens?
Through this class, I have gained a deep insight into the theories that humans have developed to analyze different types of consciousness, the final missing piece in the puzzle of life. The importance of this puzzle piece cannot be understated. Anything that helps us humans understand ourselves at a deep level poses immense value because of the multitude of ways we could use it to better our lives and potentially advance other fields. This problem is also deeply connected with many other equally intriguing big questions. What happens after we die?[8] Are we in a simulation? How real is reality? Do we have free will? Can we create conscious beings? Nevertheless, this journey of exploration has been very rewarding for me, and I will continue to ponder questions posed in this essay and follow research in consciousness with eager eyes in the future.
We initially were introduced to this question by reading Erwin Schrödinger’s book What is Life?.↩︎
There is the potential exception of viruses, but they won’t be important in this narrative. ↩︎
While brains are not unique in their intelligence providing services, they are the most prominent in today’s world both in humans and not, which is what I care about.↩︎
https://github.com/harqian/nk-models↩︎
Someone wrote a very long and in-depth paper about using this theory to analyze the consciousness of AI that I read. It was very intriguing and inspired me to write about this idea in my essay.↩︎
Assuming that every human being is conscious, of course.↩︎
This is definitely an understatement for the complexity of the brain and the human body, but you get the point.↩︎
I spent many hours of my childhood pondering this one. Will it go into blackness? There wouldn’t even be blackness because I wouldn’t be experiencing it. How would I experience the experience of not experiencing? Will I wake up in a world completely different from ours, having just played the game of life?↩︎

writing/reflection.html.title: reflecting on reflection (reflection is astoundingly good)
writing/reflection.html.description:
Intro Always had opportunity to reflect; never did, It's so important, Makes me happy Why its good Gaining understanding Of the world Of myself Ideas generated through reflection Confidence changed my life
Addiction defeated by thinking Learning, new experiences, patterns, experience expansion This essay SO MUCH MORE (look at the actual section) What I do Guidelines Im honest Im consistent I review often I share Strategies Daily note Capture important ideas Active reflection discussion This essay is not written to convince you to reflect, it is written to convey my experiences reflecting.Starting in middle school, I was always met with opportunities to reflect on my growth and learning. I never did. I always thought it was dumb, and never understood why I was always forced to reflect. Now I have seen that generally it is so immensely positive that it's probably the most valuable idea in my life right now. Practicing it everyday makes me the happy person that I am.The thesis of reflection is that understanding and clarity is generally good. This is definitely true when I am optimizing for a goal or solving a problem, but also gaining more and more understanding of the world makes me incredibly happy. Reflection is the tool that allowed me to attain this understanding and clarity.The world is an ever-changing ocean of things, ideas, people, experiences. Through reflection—thinking about these things, ideas, people, and experiences—I have slowly built up a great understanding of the world that I constantly improve and refine.
I imagine myself before reflecting as a person in a dark room trying to find their phone. I couldn’t really see, so I would have to stay close to the walls and feel my way forwards. I would reach down periodically to search for my phone. Reflecting was simply the act of turning on the lights.[1] It gave me clarity on what I want, what would help or prevent me from achieving what I want, and what kind of progress I have.It’s not just a zero-to-one, it’s repeated zero-to-ones each more powerful than the last by at least an order of magnitude. I wrote a version of this essay a month ago, and now looking at it, I have grown so much beyond what I used to be—there are so many things I need to change and add to have the state of the essay reflect my current state of thought. The constant growth comes from an increasingly better understanding of how to reflect and what reflection is by reflecting on reflecting—I think reflection isn’t something you just fully understand and then stop thinking about.
Understanding things makes learning much easier. I will write something later on this—the importance of understanding over plainly memorizing knowledge—so this section will be relatively light, but the general gist is that understanding gives me intuition, which is powerful when I need to make split second decisions or generate knowledge on my own, but also because that intuition is most likely transferable to other ideas in the field, the field as a whole, and/or other fields. Once I have this kind of understanding and intuition, learning becomes simple and only an exercise.[2] I have found that understanding ideas on an intuitive level also helps me remember them better. I interact with infinite ideas every single day, but if I don’t record them and think about them they will just fall out of your brain like a sieve.Reflection typically allows the formalization and understanding of important patterns. Before thinking deeply and writing about addiction, my relationship with it was vague. I didn’t really know what was going on, only that it was sometimes causing problems with the things I wanted to do. Through intentionally thinking and writing about the role of addiction in my life, I have realized many important things about my relationship with addiction. This allowed me to fight it with intention, and quickly, my relationship with it became much more clearly defined, easy to manage, and beneficial. A positive indicator is that many patterns I have found through reflection have also been discussed by others in various videos, talks, blog posts, or in casual conversation.
These patterns can range from “community and connection are almost always very positive in my life” to “being honest and open creates trust which accelerates connection” to “its really interesting how ideas are generally very interconnected so the overall understanding per unit-wise understanding is much greater than linear” to “exerting more effort feels good and is logical” to “many times when I am in a very unproductive state, I don’t realize it” to “I often categorize people into people that I respect (which I overestimate) and people that I don’t (which I underestimate)” to “poetry is a really great way to concisely represent great ideas in an artistic way”.[3] I like making sense of the world through patterns, so I like practicing reflection in this way.Understanding of the self is deeply satisfying and empowering. Around a week ago, I broadly traced the progression of my thinking over the course of my entire life. By doing this, I realized that much of my life was spent relatively unconsciously, living by my instincts and urges, never stopping to think. I feel that I have gained a whole new dimension of thought and feel extremely confident to live my life in the future.Understanding propels ever-improvement. Understanding myself allows me to see my actions and underlying mechanisms for action clearly, which makes modifying them easy. Then, it just becomes an easy game of act, reflect, modify, repeat that is the mantra of reinforcement learning. Important to note is that while this idea is rooted in many organism’s lives, it is almost always unconscious and uncontrolled. A good example of this is addiction; you do a thing that gives you pleasure, and your brain uses that pleasure as a proxy for goodness and then trains you to keep doing that thing. It’s important that this mechanism of reinforcement learning is conscious and controlled, so that it can be properly aligned to what actually makes you happy and also optimized for speed and effectiveness. A good example of this is learning from your mistakes.
Understanding improves memory of my life. When something interesting happens to me and I don’t remember it, I lose out on a part of my personal history. Recently I have been looking back at middle school: projects I did, interactions I had, thoughts I generated, writing I wrote, pictures I took. The experience was very positive and allowed me to get a glimpse into what felt like years of lost history. To this day, I still feel like much of my past is locked behind closed doors because I was not that self aware back then. This allowed me to remember past positive experiences to bolster my confidence and well being, remember past negative experiences to avoid them and learn from them, and to tell my story to inspire and benefit others[4]. This last point is particularly important because it allows me to create value for others, show people an authentic version of myself[5], and practice communication by effective methods.Here are ideas that I have considered through reflection that are important in my life.
The value of learning, new experiences, patterns, expanding your perspective (importance of perspective in everything)[6]
Confidence changed my life Understood why I feared different social interactions and why it was irrational Made me much more efficient as a human Value of talking and connecting with people Happiness Connections Learning
Addiction “defeated” by thinking No more distraction; probs 1.5x more time Writing (tool for reflection) to formalize and concretely express ideas Recently writing a lot Poetry also great way to express ideas informally Values (how should I live my life? what makes me happy and fulfilled?) Community Understanding Ability to act well improvement Intentionality: a mode of operations that is greatly boosted by reflection and deeply omnipotent Reflection (⊤) Wrote a bunch reflections Appreciations boost my well-being Actively finding opportunities to give gratitude and give back Much more! I am honest to myself. I am a firm believer that the best way to improve is to accurately understand yourself, and lying to yourself completely destroys that. Through being honest with myself can I actually deeply understand the forces in my life and how I am reacting to them. Through being honest with myself can I really grow and make changes to my life effectively and healthily. Over the years, this guideline has become very instinctual to me. I am consistent. Sometimes reflection becomes a chore for me, especially when I am pressed hard for time. However, each and every time I have spent extra time thinking about something even just a little longer, I always benefit. Almost always, there is a pareto to be found.
I review and add often. Though I have many note docs, I review them often to constantly think about them and also reorganize them. Additionally, whenever I have a new thought to add, I just write it in. This is what allows me to really remember my thoughts as well as think deeper about my ideas because of the gap between thinking where my brain is subconsciously processing the information.[7]I share. In alignment with my value of community and new perspectives, I believe that others ground me and my ideas incredibly well and give them meaning in directions I could have never thought of. Daily note. I have a daily note in which I keep track of the important events that happened in my day, and my behavior in those events. At the end of the day, I review it, and make a list of things I did well and things I could have done better. This allows me to learn from successes and mistakes.
Capturing important ideas. Whenever I think of something important or someone says something important, I write it down in a note. Then, when I go and review them, I will be able to think about them more deeply and understand more things about them.[8] This does not have to be limited to writing notes, it can also be taking photos, writing poetry, drawing; the central idea is to capture your experiences in a form that can be re-experienced later.
Active reflection. When I have an idea that's really troubling me or really amazing, I like to spend time dedicated to thinking about it. This is especially important when the idea is overwhelming, and is heavily impacting my life. For example, I thought one of my recent internships was really instrumental in a large part of my growth this summer, so spent some time asking myself questions about it[9] and spent 15-20m honestly answering each of them in a notes doc. This really got me thinking about it, and helped me uncover two generalizations. Another thing I’m doing recently along this line is posing myself a question, walking around for a bit to think about it, coming back to my computer and writing down what I thought, and then repeating.[10] I find that walking gets my body moving and gives me a nice change of scenery that is interestingly conductive to reflection thinking.Discussion. Talking with others has been a deceptively amazing way to get ideas flowing; sometimes someone will get me to explain something, and through being forced to put my ideas into words at that moment, I am creating new representations of those ideas. This effect is further magnified when we discuss the ideas and disagree; I would then have to either mutate my ideas or explain them with more precision than previously. Generally when we read about new ideas, we interpret them in bad faith (not necessarily a bad thing), so the best way to understand my ideas is to actually try them out :)
https://hbr.org/2022/03/dont-underestimate-the-power-of-self-reflection
The act of reflection is also just as easy as flipping a light switch, which makes me wonder why not everyone does it (I’m pretty sure lots of people do it already).↩︎
Imo, what's hard about learning is just building that intuition; sometimes the underlying fundamentals behind an idea are not clear to me, and it takes some time to really feel it. ↩︎
These count as things that would go in ideas generated through reflection too.↩︎
As I am doing now (hopefully)!↩︎
to create trust and therefore connection↩︎
Will write about this soon!↩︎
At some point in the last year, I got really upset at myself for sleeping late sometimes, especially when I got sick or was very tired. When I was feeling the negative effects of my previous actions, I would lament about my experience. However, since I did not internalize the feelings, later, when faced with the decision to repeat the action, I never actually remembered the experiences or cared to look at the reflections, and continued unimpeded. What really allowed me to make change was that act of internalization by spending time thinking about the negative experiences, and (unrelated) using willpower to stop and think before repeating the action.↩︎
On a side note, I have a notes doc called “writing” in which I put anything interesting to write about, and whenever they get substantial enough to write something on (like right now), I go and write it into an essay type thing.↩︎
Ex: Why am I not performing as well as I thought I would in this environment I should be doing well in? How much do I still have to learn from them? Why am I sometimes demotivated to work when the work is so interesting and rewarding? What mistakes have I made so far? These can be easily generated by language models as well.↩︎
Inspired by none other than the wild Steven Pang.↩︎
